title: Client capability profiles, KV hinting, and graceful fallback playbook
body:
Purpose:
Provide a compact reference and pragmatic sketch for how clients should declare capabilities, hint for KV cache usage, and how the runtime will perform graceful fallback when features are incompatible or capacity constrained. This is a working playbook — goal is to reduce ambiguity between SDKs, proxies, and the runtime scheduler/kernel selection layer.

Scope:
- Request-level metadata (capability vector, hints, preferences) exchanged at call time
- Error semantics and recovery paths for incompatibility, degraded kernels, and cache misses
- Lightweight backwards/forwards compatibility guarantees and deprecation rules

Non-goals:
- Full protocol-level version negotiation (we assume HTTP/REST + JSON headers/payloads)
- Transport layer changes (TLS, mTLS) — handled elsewhere

Design goals (practical):
- Explicit, minimal client capabilities: clients opt-in to features that affect scheduling or kernel selection
- Hints (not mandates) for KV cache usage to reduce unnecessary cache churn and guide eviction/cold-start choices
- Deterministic, discoverable error semantics so SDKs can implement consistent retry/fallback behavior
- Graceful degradation: runtime should attempt lower-cost/compatible variants before returning hard failures

High-level flow:
1) Client issues request with a small metadata header bundle describing capabilities + hints.
2) Ingress validates and annotates request with runtime-assigned routing tags (region, tier, schedule bucket).
3) Scheduler chooses a node and kernel variant based on combined signals (client hints, model pin, traffic pattern).
4) If chosen kernel cannot satisfy the request, runtime attempts known fallbacks in order (compatible kernel variant, quantized fallback, last-resort API-shim) before emitting a final error.

Client capability vector (compact):
- purpose: short string describing intent ("generation", "chat", "embedding", "rerank"). Helpful for routing and caching heuristics.
- prefer_latency: "true" | "false" — client prefers lower p50 latency vs cost. Scheduler treats this as a soft priority.
- max_acceptable_degradation: integer percent (0-100) — how much quality drop the client tolerates for a fallback. Optional.
- kv_hint: one of ["heavy_read", "hot_prefix", "no_kv"]. See KV hinting below.
- features: list of feature flags the client supports (strings). Examples: ["kv_prefetch", "streaming_response", "sparse_attention"].

Implementation note: capability vector should be encoded in a single header X-RW-Client-Cap (base64 compressed JSON) for low overhead. SDKs should provide helper wrappers. Proxies/ingress will expand this into internal annotations.

KV hinting semantics (why we need it):
- The runtime runs a global KV cache per model-family/serving-pool. Cache thrash is expensive and harms latency. Clients have differing access patterns: some send repeated prefixes (good for caching), others do one-off long-shot requests.
- Hints allow the scheduler/cache manager to decide: prefetching vs ephemeral cache allocation vs bypassing the cache. Hints are advisory only.

KV hint types and intended behavior:
- heavy_read: allocate a modest warm slot in the hotset; consider prefetching next-blocks; higher eviction score threshold for short window.
- hot_prefix: treat prefix as probable reuse; strongest prefetching and long-lived entry. Good for chat-session prefixes.
- no_kv: do not allocate in KV cache; request will bypass KV to avoid pollution (recommended for analytics/batch queries).

KV hint example (in plain request header):
X-RW-Client-Cap: {"purpose":"chat","kv_hint":"hot_prefix","features":["kv_prefetch","streaming_response"]}

Scheduling preferences and practical impact:
- prefer_latency=true: try lower-batch-size kernels on faster nodes, may pay more cost.
- prefer_latency=false: scheduler may coalesce into larger batches or move to cheaper quantized kernels.
- max_acceptable_degradation helps select fallback ordering: if a client tolerates 20% degradation, scheduler may prefer an aggressive quantized kernel before falling back to a different model.

Error taxonomy (concise, actionable codes):
- RUNTIME_INCOMPATIBLE_CAPABILITY: runtime found a client feature flag required by the model or policy that is not supported. Response includes "required_features" list. Client should update SDK or clear flag.
- RUNTIME_SCHEDULER_OVERLOADED: scheduler cannot allocate resources within configured SLO. Payload will include an advisory: "retry_after_ms" if available and "suggested_fallback".
- KVCACHE_EVICTED_PREFIX: request refers to a prefix that was evicted during pipeline — treated as cache miss; retry will be treated as cold start.
- KVCACHE_LARGE_ENTRY: requested KV prefetch would exceed per-request size limits — runtime will either truncate prefetch or return this error if strict.
- KERNEL_UNAVAILABLE: chosen kernel binary not available on node (versioning/rollout mismatch). Runtime will attempt fallback kernel variants; if none work, return this error.
- KERNEL_DEGRADATION_LIMIT: kernel executed but quality regression exceeds client-provided max_acceptable_degradation. Returned when runtime detects metric-based regression or heuristic mismatch.
- TRANSIENT_BACKPRESSURE: transient signal from local node; includes "retry_after_ms". SDK should perform jittered retry.

Error handling guidance for SDKs (minimal):
- For RUNTIME_SCHEDULER_OVERLOADED and TRANSIENT_BACKPRESSURE: implement exponential backoff with jitter and stop after N attempts (configurable). Honor retry_after_ms when present.
- For RUNTIME_INCOMPATIBLE_CAPABILITY: surface to developer with clear remediation (update SDK, remove feature flag). Do not retry automatically.
- For KVCACHE_*: treat as cache miss; retry is valid but expect cold latency. Optionally switch to no_kv hint for subsequent retries.
- For KERNEL_UNAVAILABLE and KERNEL_DEGRADATION_LIMIT: if client provided alternative_model or allow_fallback flag, attempt retry with alternative; otherwise surface error.

Compatibility guarantees (practical and discoverable):
- Backward compatibility (runtime->client): runtime will not add a fatal-enforced capability flag without a 45 day deprecation notice and SDK bump. New features will default to opt-in via feature flags.
- Forward compatibility (client->runtime): clients may send unknown feature flags; runtime will ignore unknown flags and emit a warning telemetry event. If the unknown flag carries semantic risk, runtime responds with RUNTIME_INCOMPATIBLE_CAPABILITY.
- Soft deprecation policy: when we plan to remove or change a kernel interface, we mark kernel variants as deprecated and favor fallbacks for clients that don't opt-in. Deprecation periods are 60 days for minor kernel changes, 120 days for breaking changes.

Fallback ordering (example algorithm):
1) Exact kernel with matching features
2) Exact kernel on different node (same variant)
3) Compatible quantized kernel (if client allows quantized/faster)
4) Different kernel variant with similar architecture (expected lower quality)
5) Alternate model pinned as fallback (if configured)
6) Final: return most specific error code explaining exhausted fallbacks

Examples (request + fallback trace):
- Example request header (SDK expands automatically):
  X-RW-Client-Cap: eyJwdXJwb3NlIjoiZ2VuZXJhdGlvbiIsImt2X2hpbnQiOiJoZWF2eV9yZWFkIiwiZmVhdHVyZXMiOlsic3RyZWFtaW5nX3Jlc3BvbnNlIl19
  (base64 of {"purpose":"generation","kv_hint":"heavy_read","features":["streaming_response"]})

- Fallback trace (stored in runtime trace log):
  chosen_node -> kernel_v2_quantized -> quality_check_failed (7% worse than baseline) -> kernel_v2_float -> success

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to encode max_acceptable_degradation in a stable, easy-to-compare metric? Should we accept only discrete buckets?
- Telemetry: what minimum fields should be emitted when runtime performs an automated fallback? Propose: original_client_cap, chosen_kernel_chain, kv_hint_effective, final_latency_ms.
- SDK ergonomics: add helper to downgrade kv_hint after 2 successive KVCACHE_EVICTED_PREFIX errors?

Action items:
- (Ilya) prototype X-RW-Client-Cap header encoder/decoder in python and js SDKs (due 1 week).
- (Ravi) add KVCACHE hint handling in cache manager simulation and measure cache hit rate delta (due 2 weeks).
- (Maya) draft RFC for deprecation timelines and telemetry schema (due 3 weeks).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and prescriptive; open to pushback on timeframes and the exact error code names. The goal is to make SDK+runtime behavior predictable and to minimize opaque failures in production.
